subject: Number of Detections Per Stratum - Line Transect Survey Design

messages.author: 8c434d4aad54fb95
messages.subject: Number of Detections Per Stratum - Line Transect Survey Design
parts:
Hello all, 

     I am working on a line transect survey design to estimate bird nest density over a relatively large area (about 716,251 square kilometers). From prior studies, there is some knowledge of the current nest density gradient in the area. I am wondering if it will be beneficial to create several stratum based on the varying levels of density. My understanding of the benefit of this is that it can potentially improve precision of the density estimate because variation in the number of detections between lines within the stratum is lowered. If we are interested in a density estimate at the study area level, not stratum level, would it be okay if there were not 60-80 detections per stratum, but approximately 60-80 when pooling across stratum? And would there also need to be 15-20 replications within each stratum or just pooled across stratum? 
     It would also be beneficial if more effort could be focused on the areas of higher density. Does this introduce bias because areas of fewer detections will be confounded with areas of less effort? 

     To summarize, my questions are: 
     1. When dividing a study area into several stratum, do there need to be a significant number of detections per stratum (60-80) if we are interested only in                 density at the level of the study area (not at the stratum level)? Or is about 60-80 detections when pooled across stratum enough? 
     2. When dividing a study area into several stratum, do there need to be 15-20 replicates per stratum if we are interested only in density at the level of the 
         study area (not at the stratum level)? Or is 15-20 replicates when pooled across stratum enough?
     3. Does lower effort in stratum with known lower densities produce a bias estimate of density when estimating density for the entire study area? 


     Thank you in advance for any interest and input!

-Elaine Gallenberg

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Number of Detections Per Stratum - Line Transect Survey Design
parts:
Elaine

All valuable things to consider when designing a distance sampling survey.  If you have a copy of Buckland et al. (2015) to hand, have a look at Section 2.3 for a discussion of the subject.

In short, you can use stratification to accomplish one of two purposes: a) estimate density in sub-areas (strata) of your study area or b) increase precision of your estimate across the entire study area as you note.  The suggested sample sizes for number of detections and number of transects applies to the area at which you are performing the estimation, in your case the entire study area.

Regarding effort allocation based upon presumed densities:  it is common to allocate greater effort in areas of higher density.  There are drawbacks to this allocation scheme.  With low effort in areas of low density, estimates of abundance in these areas will be imprecise.  That might not be a problem if the low-density areas are small in size.  But if low density areas are large (high quality habitat is scarce) then these low density areas might constitute a large proportion of the population in the study area (and it will be poorly estimated) (Section 2.3.1 Buckland et al. (2015)).  The result of the effort allocation scheme is unlikely to produce bias in the point estimates, but there the situation as I have described could cause precision to suffer.

If the answer to this question is critical to your investigation, you might consider conducting some contrasting simulations in Distance for Windows or the DSsim R package.

Buckland, S. T., E. A. Rexstad, T. A. Marques, and C. S. Oedekoven. 2015. Distance Sampling: Methods and Applications. Springer.
